common_name: Queen Lime Zinnia (Trendy Muted Lime-Green Cut Flower Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost in warm soil; Queen Lime is grown chiefly for cut-flower arranging, valued for its unusual muted, dusty lime-green blooms that pair well with almost any other flower color.

directions: Direct sow after frost in warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Queen Lime has become a favorite of cut-flower growers and florists for its unusual soft, dusty lime-green double blooms, sometimes blushed with pink or rose at the petal tips, a muted color palette that blends easily with nearly any other cut flower rather than competing with it. The tall, sturdy stems make excellent cut flowers with a long vase life, and regular cutting or deadheading keeps the plant producing new blooms over a long summer season. Like other zinnias it thrives in heat and is a strong pollinator and butterfly magnet, though good air circulation helps reduce powdery mildew in humid climates.
sources: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

common_name: Bonanza Marigold (Compact Uniform French Marigold Series)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Bonanza is a compact, uniform French marigold series bred for bedding and container use, flowering quickly from seed.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Bonanza is a widely grown, compact French marigold series bred for a uniform, tidy, mounding habit and quick, heavy flowering from seed, making it a reliable choice for bedding displays, edging, and containers where consistent size and abundant bicolor or solid gold, orange, and red-toned blooms are wanted. It flowers quickly after sowing and continues through the heat of summer with good tolerance for poor soil and drought once established. Deadheading spent blooms encourages continued flowering, and the pungent foliage is generally avoided by deer and rabbits.

common_name: Durango Marigold (Early-Flowering Compact French Marigold Series)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost, or start indoors a few weeks early for earlier bloom; Durango is an early-flowering, weather-tolerant French marigold series with large flowers relative to its compact plant size.

directions: Direct sow or transplant into well-drained, average soil in full sun. Durango is a popular French marigold series known for flowering earlier from seed than many older marigold types, producing unusually large, fully double flowers in gold, orange, and red bicolor tones on a compact, weather-resistant plant that holds up well in rain and wind. It performs reliably through summer heat and needs only routine deadheading to keep flowering strongly. Like other marigolds it is drought-tolerant once established and its pungent foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits, making it a dependable bedding and container annual.

common_name: Sonata Cosmos (Compact Dwarf Bedding Cosmos Series)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost in average soil; overly rich soil reduces blooms. Sonata is a compact, dwarf cosmos series bred for bedding displays and containers, staying shorter and sturdier than tall heirloom cosmos types.

directions: Direct sow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, since overly fertile soil produces excess foliage at the expense of flowers. Sonata is a dwarf cosmos series bred to stay compact and sturdy, avoiding the tall, floppy growth of many heirloom cosmos varieties, which makes it much better suited to bedding displays, borders, and containers where a shorter, self-supporting plant is needed. It produces the same large, daisy-like flowers in white, pink, and crimson over a long summer season, drawing bees and butterflies, and its shorter stature means it rarely needs staking even in open, windy sites. Deadheading spent blooms extends the flowering season into fall.

common_name: Mammoth Russian Sunflower (Classic Giant Single-Stem Sunflower)

planting.note: Sow after the last frost when soil is warm; Mammoth Russian is a classic giant heirloom sunflower producing a single towering stalk topped by an enormous seed head, grown as much for edible, harvestable seed as for ornamental impact.

directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Mammoth Russian is one of the oldest and most iconic giant sunflower heirlooms, reliably reaching ten to twelve feet or more on a single sturdy stalk topped by a massive, heavy flower head that matures into a dense disc of large, striped seeds prized for roasting, snacking, and bird feed. Because of its impressive height and heavy seed head, it benefits from a somewhat sheltered site out of strong wind, and very tall specimens may need staking. Once the back of the flower head turns yellow-brown and petals drop, the seed head can be cut and hung to dry before threshing out the seeds for harvest or leaving it up for birds.
